sources.news_title: Trump says Islamic State group leader was killed in a joint US-Nigerian mission
sources.text:
Trump says Islamic State group leader was killed in a joint US-Nigerian mission
Trump says Islamic State group leader was killed in a joint US-Nigerian mission
WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. and Nigerian forces killed a leader of the Islamic State group in Nigeria in a mission carried out Friday, U.S. President Donald Trump said.
The U.S. military released footage Saturday said to show airstrikes in Nigeria targeting the Islamic State group.
Trump announced the joint operation in Africa’s most populous country in a late-night social media post. He said Abu Bakr al-Mainuki was second-in-command of the Islamic State group globally and “thought he could hide in Africa, but little did he know we had sources who kept us informed on what he was doing.”
Al-Mainuki was viewed as the key figure in IS organizing and finance, and had been plotting attacks against the United States and its interests, according to an official who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to share sensitive information.
Nigerian President Bola Tinubu confirmed the operation and said Al-Mainuki was killed alongside “several of his lieutenants, during a strike on his compound in the Lake Chad Basin.”
The joint operation is the latest by both countries since their new security partnership that kicked off last year after Trump claimed Christians were being targeted in Nigeria’s security crisis and threatened U.S. military intervention. Residents and security analysts have said Nigeria’s security crisis affects both Christians, predominant in the south, and Muslims, who are the majority in the north.
According to the spokesperson for the Nigerian military task force that carried out the Friday operation, the mission was a “highly complex precision air-land operation” and was carried out during three hours of darkness early Saturday without any casualties or loss of assets.
“His elimination represents the single most consequential counterterrorism outcome” in the region since the inception of the operation in 2015, Sani Uba, the spokesperson for the task force, said in a statement.
United Nations experts in their latest report said IS had intensified efforts in West Africa, citing more than 500 attacks between January and October last year.
Questions over Al-Mainuki’s exact status in IS
Born in Nigeria’s Borno province in 1982, al-Mainuki took the helm of the IS branch in West Africa after his predecessor, Mamman Nur, was killed in 2018, according to the Counter Extremism Project, which tracks militant groups.
Al-Mainuki was based in the Sahel area, the monitoring group said, adding that it is believed that he fought in Libya when IS was active in the North African nation more than a decade ago. He was sanctioned by the U.S. in 2023.
Trump, in his social media announcement, said Al-Mainuki was “second in command globally,” hiding in Africa, a claim that some analysts say is off the mark. The Nigerian military, in a statement, also said intelligence shows that earlier this year, Al-Mainuki might have been “elevated to the position of Head of the General Directorate of States, placing him the second most senior leader within the ISIS global hierarchy.”
U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth also said Al-Mainuki was the senior ISIS General Directorate of Provinces Emir — “the number two for ISIS globally — responsible for overseeing the planning of attacks, directing the hostage-taking and managing financial operations.”
There is no way to verify his position within IS independently. Analysts say Al-Mainuki was the deputy to Abu Musab al-Barnawi, the leader of the Islamic State West African Province who was reported to have died in 2021. He is regarded as one of the central proponents of the formation of ISWAP, after its split with Boko Haram in 2016.
“If confirmed, the killing of Al-Mainuki is huge because this is the first time a security agency has killed someone this high in the ranking of ISWAP,” Malik Samuel, a senior researcher at Good Governance Africa who specializes in insurgent groups in Nigeria, said.
“The potential to cause chaos within the group is also there because the operation must have been carried out in the heart of ISWAP’s fortified base, which is very difficult to access.”
Trump in December directed U.S. forces to launch strikes against the Islamic State group in Nigeria, though he released little detail then about the impact.
US and Nigeria step up joint operations
The Nigerian military said the operation was a result of recently formed U.S.-Nigeria partnership and intelligence-sharing efforts. Samalia Uba, the military spokesperson, said in a statement that the operation has also “disrupted a violent terrorist network that endangered Nigeria and the broader West African region.”
Nigeria has been battling multiple armed groups, including at least two affiliated with IS, as it has grappled with a multifaceted security crisis. IS affiliates in Africa have emerged as some of the continent’s most active militant groups following the collapse of the so-called IS caliphate in Syria and Iraq in 2017.
The U.S. in February sent troops to the West African nation to help advise its military, and in March, the U.S. also deployed drones there after Trump’s allegations about Christians being targeted in Nigeria.
The Friday night operation was the latest instance in a string of covert missions abroad that Trump has announced this year, starting with the stunning overnight raid in January to capture and remove Venezuela’s then-leader Nicolás Maduro and whisk him to the U.S., followed nearly two months later by the launch of strikes that kicked off the war with Iran.
___
Adetayo reported from Lagos, Nigeria. Associated Press writers Dyepkazah Shibayan in Abuja, Konstantin Toropin in Washington and Samy Magdy in Cairo contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: US and Nigerian forces kill senior ISIS commander, Trump says
sources.text:
US and Nigerian forces killed a senior ISIS commander on Friday, President Donald Trump said, in an operation he claimed had “greatly diminished” the militant group’s power.
“Tonight, at my direction, brave American forces and the Armed Forces of Nigeria flawlessly executed a meticulously planned and very complex mission to eliminate the most active terrorist in the world from the battlefield,” Trump said in a Truth Social post late Friday ET.
The president named the target as “Abu-Bilal al-Minuki, second in command of ISIS globally,” adding: “He will no longer terrorize the people of Africa, or help plan operations to target Americans.”
Trump did not specify where the attack happened. He said al-Minuki “thought he could hide in Africa, but little did he know we had sources who kept us informed on what he was doing.”
According to documents from the US Office of Foreign Assets Control, al-Minuki was born in 1982 in the northeastern Nigerian state of Borno, which borders Cameroon, Chad and Niger.
Al-Minuki has long been a focus of Nigeria’s military operations. In 2024, he was among the suspected ISWAP/Boko Haram commanders killed in the Birnin Gwari forest area of northern Kaduna State.
On Sunday, Bayo Onanuga, a spokesperson for President Tinubu, issued a statement acknowledging the earlier claim of al-Minuki’s death in 2024, but explained that the previous listing was “a case of mistaken identity or misattribution.” Onanuga also added that the Birnin Gwari area was never within al-Minuki’s established operational hub. “This time, however, security and military authorities maintain a far higher level of confidence,” he said.
Trump thanked the Nigerian government for its cooperation, and said “with his removal, ISIS’s global operation is greatly diminished.”
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said that US forces had for months “hunted this top ISIS leader in Nigeria who was killing Christians, and we killed him — and his entire posse.”
“Operations like last night’s demonstrate the exceptional lethality, patience and skill of U.S. forces, amplified alongside willing and capable partners, to address shared threats,” Hegseth added.
Nigeria’s State House, the office of the President of Nigeria, also confirmed the operation in a statement. Nigerian and US forces “conducted a daring joint operation that dealt a heavy blow to the ranks of the Islamic State,” it said.
“Early assessments confirm the elimination of the wanted IS senior leader, Abu-Bilal Al-Manuki, also known as Abu-Mainok, along with several of his lieutenants, during a strike on his compound in the Lake Chad Basin,” it added.
Nigerian President Bola Ahmed Tinubu thanked Trump in a statement Saturday morning.
“Nigeria appreciates this partnership with the United States in advancing our shared security objectives,” he wrote on social media. “I extend my sincere gratitude to President Trump for his leadership and unwavering support in this effort.”
Daniel Bwala, a spokesperson for Nigerian President Tinubu, confirmed to CNN that “the leader of this terrorist organization ISWAP had been under surveillance for some time,” adding that “when he was identified and located around Lake Chad, both the US and Nigerian government felt it was the right time to strike.”
Bwala said that the “successful operation” is proof of the collaboration between the US and Nigeria.
“Nigeria still insists that there is no Christian genocide taking place in Nigeria,” he said, insisting that terrorists target people of “all faiths.”
It is not the first fatal strike Trump has ordered on alleged ISIS militants in Nigeria, whom he has accused of persecuting Christians in the West African country.
In December, Trump said he had directed a “powerful and deadly strike against ISIS” in northwestern Nigeria, who he said had been killing innocent Christians.
A month prior, Trump said he was contemplating military action in response to what he claimed was a “mass slaughter” of Christians by Islamist insurgents.
The Nigerian government at the time rejected claims that it is not doing enough to protect Christians from violence, saying it was bewildered by Trump’s suggestion of a potential military intervention.
Christians and Muslims make up the two main religious groups in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous nation and home to an estimated 237.5 million.
Experts and analysts say the reality on the ground is nuanced, with both groups falling victim to attacks by radical Islamists.
The country has grappled for years with deep-rooted security problems driven by various factors, including religiously motivated attacks.
Observers say other violent conflicts arise from communal and ethnic tensions, as well as disputes between farmers and herders over limited access to land and water resources.
This story has been updated.
CNN’s Kevin Liptak, Kara Fox and Nimi Princewell contributed reporting.

sources.news_title: ISIS No. 2 Abu-Bilal al-Minuki killed in Nigeria
sources.text:
Trump, Nigeria claim killing of senior ISIS leader Abu-Bilal al-Minuki
Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox
ABUJA/WASHINGTON – A senior leader of the ISIS militant group has been killed in a joint operation by US and Nigerian forces in the West African country, the two countries’ presidents said.
Under US sanctions since 2023, Abu-Bilal al-Minuki was the second in command of ISIS worldwide, according to US President Donald Trump and the Nigerian military.
First announcing the killing in a post on the Truth Social platform, Mr Trump said: “Tonight, at my direction, brave American forces and the armed forces of Nigeria flawlessly executed a meticulously planned and very complex mission to eliminate the most active terrorist in the world from the battlefield.”
The Nigerian defence forces said al-Minuki was a “senior ISIS leader and one of the world’s most active terrorists”.
It described him as an “operational and strategic figure who provided guidance to ISIS entities outside Nigeria on matters relating to media operations, economic warfare and the development and manufacturing of weapons, explosives and drones”.
“Our determined Nigerian armed forces, working closely with the armed forces of the United States, conducted a daring joint operation that dealt a heavy blow to the ranks of the Islamic State,” Nigerian President Bola Tinubu said, using another name for the terror group.
He said in his statement that al-Minuki, also known as Abu-Mainok, was killed “along with several of his lieutenants during a strike on his compound in the Lake Chad Basin”, a restive region straddling Niger, Chad and Cameroon.
The operation was “a meticulously planned and highly complex precision air-land operation” carried out on May 16 between midnight and 4am (7am and 11am Singapore time), the Nigerian army said.
Nigerian military spokesman Sani Uba said the operation followed intelligence that al-Minuki and his cell had established a “concealed and fortified enclave” at a remote village in the Borno State in the north-east, the epicentre of a 17-year armed insurgency.
The Nigerian military sees al-Minuki’s death as removing a “critical node through which ISIS coordinated and directed operations across different regions of the world”.
Nigeria has long been battling jihadist insurgents, including regional offshoots of the ISIS organisation as well as extremist rival Boko Haram. It has also carried out strikes and operations against non-ideological violent gangs of criminals known as “bandits”.
Since late 2025, the Nigerian government has been under pressure from the US, which has accused it of not doing enough to combat the militant threat.
On Christmas Day, the US, in collaboration with the Nigerian authorities, carried out air strikes in north-western Sokoto state targeting fighters from terror affiliate ISIS-Sahel, usually active in neighbouring Niger.
Washington has since deployed hundreds of troops to Nigeria to support and train its forces.
Mr Tinubu thanked Mr Trump for his “leadership and unwavering support in this effort”, adding that he looked “forward to more decisive strikes against all terrorist enclaves across the nation”.
No soldiers or assets were lost during the operation, according to the Nigerian army.
Al-Minuki oversaw ISIS-linked operations across the Sahel and West Africa, including attacks against “ethnic and religious minority communities”, the Nigerian military said.
Previously a senior member of Boko Haram, which has been waging an Islamist insurgency in the region since 2009, he was linked to the 2018 Dapchi kidnapping of more than 100 schoolgirls in north-eastern Nigeria’s Yobe state.
Between March 2015 and early 2016, he also facilitated the movement of fighters to Libya to support ISIS operations in North Africa, according to the army. AFP

Who was Abu Bilal al-Minuki?
Abu-Bilal al-Minuki was born in the Borno state of Nigeria in 1982. He was designation Specially Designated Global Terrorists by the US on June 8, 2023, along with another ISIS leader Abdallah Makki Muslih al-Rufay’i of the Iraq-based ISIS.

Regional scholars have also pointed to his strained ties with Boko Haram leader Abubakar Shekau. Sometime between March 2015 and early 2016, Shekau reportedly rejected an ISIS directive to deploy fighters to Libya, the CEP website states. Al-Minuki, who at the time served as ISWAP’s Lake Chad area commander, instead facilitated the deployment. The move is said to have further deepened tensions with Shekau, who opposed efforts to strengthen cooperation with ISIS.
It remains unclear when al-Minuki rose to become the senior leader of ISIS’s al-Furqan Office, one of the group’s most active and established regional networks. These regional offices are tasked with providing ISIS affiliates with operational direction and access to international funding.

"Abu-Bilal al-Minuki, second in command of ISIS globally, thought he could hide in Africa, but little did he know we had sources who kept us informed on what he was doing," Trump added.
"He will no longer terrorize the people of Africa, or help plan operations to target Americans. With his removal, ISIS’s global operation is greatly diminished. Thank you to the Government of Nigeria for your partnership on this operation. GOD BLESS AMERICA! President DONALD J. TRUMP."
Trump did not provide details of the exact location of the operation.
But Nigerian President Bola Tinubu confirmed the operation and said Al-Minuki was killed alongside “several of his lieutenants, during a strike on his compound in the Lake Chad Basin.”
Newsweek reached out to the Pentagon via email for comment late Friday night.

Trump has previously accused Nigeria of failing to protect Christians from Islamist militants in the northwest. Nigeria has denied discriminating against any religion, saying its security forces target armed groups that attack both Christians and Muslims.
The Friday night operation was the latest instance in a string of covert missions abroad that Trump has announced this year, starting with the stunning overnight raid in January to capture and remove Venezuela’s then-leader Nicolás Maduro and whisk him to the U.S., followed nearly two months later by the launch of strikes that kicked off the war with Iran.

He was based in the Sahel area, the monitoring group said, adding that it is believed that he fought in Libya when ISIS was active in the North African nation more than a decade ago.
He was given the classification of a "specially designated global terrorist" and sanctioned by former President Joe Biden's administration in 2023, according to the U.S. Federal Register.
He was viewed as the key figure in ISIS organizing and finance, and had been plotting attacks against the United States and its interests, the Associated Press reported, citing an official who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to share sensitive information.

in December, Trump directed U.S. forces to launch strikes against the Islamic State group in Nigeria. He wrote on Truth Social that it was a "a powerful and deadly strike against ISIS Terrorist Scum in Northwest Nigeria, who have been targeting and viciously killing, primarily, innocent Christians, at levels not seen for many years."
Nigeria has been battling multiple armed groups, including at least two affiliated with Islamic, as it has grappled with a multifaceted security crisis. The U.S. in February sent troops to the West African nation to help advise its military and in March, the U.S. also deployed drones there after Trump alleged that Christians are being targeted in Nigeria’s security crisis.

In a significant announcement that reverberates across global security circles, former President Donald Trump has stated that the leader of the Islamic State group has been killed in a joint mission executed by U.S. and Nigerian forces. This claim has garnered massive attention due to its implications on international military cooperation and counterterrorism strategy, particularly in the context of the ongoing threat posed by ISIS in West Africa.
The Context: ISIS and West Africa
The Islamic State group has been a source of fear and instability in various regions, particularly in West Africa. Since its emergence, ISIS has expanded its reach through affiliate groups, increasingly threatening local populations and the broader international community. The situation has been exacerbated by the complex political landscapes in countries like Nigeria, where Boko Haram and its splinter group, the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), have caused significant humanitarian crises.
Trump’s announcement about the death of the Islamic State leader could have profound implications for security in the region and U.S. foreign policy. By eliminating high-ranking members of the group, it is hoped that there could be a decrease in attacks and a disruption of their operational capabilities.
The Joint Operation: Details and Implications
While specifics about the location and the nature of the operation remain scarce, such missions typically involve complex planning and coordination. Joint operations between U.S. and Nigerian forces are not unprecedented, but they often attract scrutiny regarding both effectiveness and the collateral impact on local civilians. In this context, questions regarding the safety of innocents and the ethical implications of military intervention arise.
The confirmation of the killing of the ISIS leader is expected to be backed by intelligence and operational evidence, which could include visual confirmations or intercepted communications. As such evidence helps validate the claim, it also serves as a reminder of the ongoing threat posed by ISIS and its affiliates.
Reactions from Global Leaders
The announcement has prompted reactions from various political figures and security experts around the world. Many view it as a positive step towards combatting terrorism, while others express caution about celebrating military successes without addressing underlying socio-political issues that fuel extremism.
U.S. officials have historically emphasized the importance of multinational efforts to combat terrorism, and Trump’s assertion positions the U.S. as a leader in global counterterrorism initiatives. However, it also raises questions about the sustainability of such victories and the need for long-term strategies that address root causes.
Analysis of the Impact on U.S. Foreign Policy
This operation falls within a broader context of U.S. foreign policy aimed at countering terrorism and fostering stability in regions affected by extremist violence. Trump’s announcement may influence public perception of his administration’s approach to national security, especially in light of previous criticisms regarding U.S. engagement in foreign conflicts.
Furthermore, the success of this operation may lead to renewed discussions about military funding, international partnerships, and the complex dynamics of foreign aid in conflict regions. How the U.S. navigates these topics in light of the operation’s outcomes will be crucial in shaping future policy decisions.
The Broader Implications of the Killing
The killing of a high-profile terrorist leader often brings about a wave of speculation regarding its impact on organizational structure within terrorist groups. History shows that the elimination of leaders can lead to both destabilization and fragmentation, as well as potential revenge operations against U.S. interests.
In the case of ISIS, analysts will be keenly observing how the group’s remaining leadership responds to this loss. Will they replace the leader quickly, or could a power vacuum emerge? The operational capabilities of the group could hinge on these factors in the following months.
Public Sentiment and Media Coverage
The media’s coverage of this announcement will play a significant role in shaping public sentiment. As the reporting unfolds, audiences will undoubtedly seek more information regarding the operation, including any potential civilian casualties, and the overall success of the mission. The narrative built around this operation will either bolster or undermine public support for U.S. military involvement in foreign conflicts.
Trump’s announcement appears poised to spike interest in security issues and counterterrorism initiatives, particularly among those concerned about the ramifications of ISIS activity in Africa and beyond.
Ensuring Accountability and Transparency
As with any military operation, accountability and transparency are vital. The U.S. government will need to provide clarity regarding the operation’s objectives, its execution, and the aftermath to ensure public trust and support. Additionally, considerations regarding civilian safety and international law must be addressed to maintain credibility in the international arena.
Furthermore, the response from Nigerian authorities and other regional partners will be crucial in framing the success of the operation. Collaborative efforts that prioritize local input and collaboration are essential in addressing the multifaceted challenges posed by terrorism.
Conclusion: A Turning Point in the Fight Against ISIS?
The announcement of the Trump Islamic State leader killed marks a critical moment in the ongoing battle against terrorism. The implications extend beyond immediate security concerns, touching on broader questions of foreign policy, military ethics, and the enduring search for peace in regions plagued by violence.
As the world watches and waits for further developments, it is clear that the fight against ISIS is far from over. This operation may serve as a reminder of the challenges that lie ahead, as well as the importance of sustained international cooperation in combating extremism.
While the death of a leader may strike a blow against a terrorist organization, the roots of extremism run deep, and addressing them will require much more than military might.

sources.news_title: Sheikh Gumi Reacts to Killing of ISIS Leader Al-Minuki, Questions Choice of Allies in Joint US Nigeria Operation
sources.text:
Islamic cleric, Ahmad Gumi, has reacted to the reported killing of Abu-Bilal al-Minuki, described as the second-in-command of ISIS worldwide, in a joint operation involving American forces and the Nigerian military.
In a Facebook post on Saturday, Gumi said that fighting terrorism is a religious duty but criticised what he described as cooperation with individuals whose “hands stained with the blood of innocent men, women, and children.”
“It’s a religious obligation to annihilate terrorists, but not with Beelzebub and hands stained with the blood of innocent men, women, and children,” he wrote.
His comments followed an announcement by US President Donald Trump, who said American forces, in collaboration with the Nigerian Armed Forces, carried out an operation that resulted in the killing of al-Minuki in Africa.
In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump said the mission was based on extensive intelligence gathering and coordinated efforts aimed at tracking the ISIS leader across the continent.
According to him, Al-Minuki was one of ISIS’s most active operatives, allegedly involved in coordinating attacks and supporting terrorist activities against both American and African targets.
Trump added that the operation would deal a major blow to ISIS operations globally and help reduce the group’s influence in Africa.
He also praised the Nigerian government and military for their role and cooperation in the joint mission.

sources.news_title: Tinubu Confirms Elimination of ISIS Commander
sources.text:
256
By Lizzy Chirkpi
President Bola Tinubu has confirmed the killing of Abu-Bilal al-Manuki, a top commander of the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), during a joint counterterrorism operation carried out by Nigerian and United States forces in the Lake Chad Basin.
In a statement issued on Saturday, President Tinubu described the operation as a major breakthrough in the ongoing fight against terrorism across Nigeria and the wider West African region.
The announcement came shortly after US President Donald Trump revealed on his Truth Social platform that the high-ranking ISIS leader had been killed in a coordinated military strike involving American troops and the Nigerian Armed Forces.
Trump described al-Manuki, also known as Abu-Mainok, as one of ISIS’ most influential global operatives who had been coordinating terrorist activities from Africa.
“Abu-Bilal al-Minuki, second in command of ISIS globally, thought he could hide in Africa, but little did he know we had sources who kept us informed on what he was doing,” Trump said.
He added that the successful operation had removed “the most active terrorist in the world from the battlefield,” noting that the development would significantly weaken ISIS operations internationally.
The US president also commended the Nigerian government and military for their cooperation and commitment to the mission.
Reacting to the development, President Tinubu praised the strong security collaboration between Nigeria and the United States, describing the operation as evidence of the effectiveness of international partnerships in combating terrorism.
“Our determined Nigerian Armed Forces, working closely with the Armed Forces of the United States, conducted a daring joint operation that dealt a heavy blow to the ranks of the Islamic State,” Tinubu stated.
According to the president, preliminary intelligence reports confirmed that al-Manuki and several of his associates were killed during a targeted strike on their hideout within the Lake Chad Basin.
Tinubu commended the professionalism, courage and resilience of the troops involved and reaffirmed Nigeria’s determination to sustain military offensives against terrorist groups operating across the region.
“I extend my sincere gratitude to President Trump for his leadership and unwavering support in this effort,” he added.
The Lake Chad Basin, covering parts of Nigeria, Niger, Chad and Cameroon, has remained a major hotspot for insurgent activities linked to Boko Haram and ISWAP.
Security experts say growing intelligence-sharing and military coordination between Nigeria and its international allies have become increasingly critical in disrupting terrorist financing, logistics and cross-border operations.
The latest operation is expected to deepen counterterrorism cooperation between Abuja and Washington, particularly in intelligence gathering, surveillance and joint military actions against extremist groups in West Africa.

sources.news_title: Trump Announces ISIS Leader Killed in Joint U.S. - Nigeria Counterterrorism Operation - Westsidevoicela
sources.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump said American and Nigerian forces killed a senior Islamic State group leader during a joint counterterrorism mission in Nigeria carried out Friday.
In a social media post late Friday night, Trump identified the militant leader as Abu Bakr al-Mainuki and described him as the Islamic State group’s second-in-command globally. Nigerian officials later confirmed the operation, saying al-Mainuki and several associates were killed during a strike in the Lake Chad Basin region.
The operation marks one of the most significant joint security missions between the United States and Nigeria since the two countries expanded military cooperation last year.
Operation
According to Nigerian military officials, the mission involved coordinated air and ground operations conducted during overnight hours.
| Detail | Information |
|---|---|
| Target | Abu Bakr al-Mainuki |
| Location | Lake Chad Basin, Nigeria |
| Operation Type | Joint U.S.-Nigeria mission |
| Timing | Early Saturday |
| Casualties Among Forces | None reported |
Nigerian President Bola Tinubu confirmed that al-Mainuki was killed alongside several of his lieutenants during a strike on his compound.
Military spokesperson Sani Uba described the mission as a “highly complex precision air-land operation” that lasted approximately three hours.
Officials said there were no reported casualties among participating forces and no military assets were lost during the operation.
Profile
U.S. officials described al-Mainuki as a major figure within the Islamic State network.
According to an American official who spoke anonymously due to the sensitivity of the operation, al-Mainuki was involved in organizing finances and coordinating activities tied to the militant group.
Trump stated that the militant leader had been plotting attacks against U.S. interests while attempting to operate from Africa.
| Background | Information |
|---|---|
| Birthplace | Borno Province, Nigeria |
| Birth Year | 1982 |
| Militant Group | Islamic State West Africa Province |
| U.S. Sanctioned | 2023 |
Analysts say al-Mainuki became a leading figure within the Islamic State West Africa Province, also known as ISWAP, following internal leadership changes several years ago.
Questions
While Trump described al-Mainuki as the Islamic State group’s second-highest global leader, some analysts said his exact rank within the organization cannot be independently verified.
The Nigerian military stated intelligence assessments suggested he may recently have been elevated to a top international leadership role inside ISIS.
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth also referred to al-Mainuki as one of the highest-ranking ISIS officials worldwide, overseeing planning, hostage operations, and finances.
However, researchers who track militant organizations cautioned that information about internal ISIS leadership structures is often difficult to confirm publicly.
Security
Nigeria has faced a prolonged security crisis involving multiple armed groups operating mainly in northern and northeastern regions of the country.
ISWAP emerged after splitting from Boko Haram in 2016 and has become one of the most active extremist groups in West Africa.
According to United Nations experts, ISIS-linked groups in West Africa carried out more than 500 attacks between January and October last year.
| Group | Area of Activity |
|---|---|
| ISWAP | Northeastern Nigeria, Lake Chad Basin |
| Boko Haram | Northern Nigeria and neighboring states |
Security analysts say the reported killing of al-Mainuki could disrupt operational planning inside ISWAP, at least temporarily.
Malik Samuel, a researcher focused on insurgent groups in Nigeria, said the operation could create instability within the organization because it reportedly targeted one of the group’s heavily fortified areas.
Partnership
The operation also highlights expanding military cooperation between the United States and Nigeria.
The two countries strengthened intelligence-sharing and counterterrorism coordination after the Trump administration increased its focus on security conditions in Nigeria last year.
In February, the United States deployed military personnel to advise Nigerian forces. Additional drone deployments followed in March as security operations expanded across affected regions.
Nigerian military officials said the latest mission was made possible through enhanced intelligence cooperation between both governments.
Officials added that the strike disrupted a militant network considered a threat to Nigeria and broader West Africa.
Outlook
Counterterrorism operations across West Africa have intensified in recent years as extremist groups continue to operate across borders in the Sahel and Lake Chad Basin regions.
Security experts caution that while the death of senior militant leaders can weaken organizations temporarily, such groups often attempt to reorganize leadership structures quickly.
Authorities in both Nigeria and the United States are expected to continue monitoring the region for possible retaliatory activity or changes in militant operations following the strike.
The joint operation represents one of the highest-profile counterterrorism actions announced by the Trump administration this year and underscores the growing international focus on militant activity in West Africa.
FAQs
Who was killed in the operation?
ISIS leader Abu Bakr al-Mainuki was killed.
Where did the operation take place?
The mission occurred in Nigeria’s Lake Chad Basin.
Who carried out the strike?
U.S. and Nigerian forces conducted the operation.
Was al-Mainuki linked to ISWAP?
Yes, he was tied to the IS West Africa branch.
Were any military casualties reported?
No casualties were reported during the mission.

George on the Weekend: ISIS Second-in-Command Killed, Israel Kills Architect of 7 October Attacks, Ebola Outbreak in Africa, Honda Reports First Ever Loss, U.S.-Nigerian Attack Kills ‘Most Active Terrorist in the World’, City Beats Chelsea
Good morning! Today is Sunday, the 17th of May, 2026 and this is the Weekend Morning Edition of GEORGE.
Against the clamor of a busy news cycle, we see a number of interesting stories that we believe our ever-curious GEORGE readers will find of interest, so let’s dive right in, shall we?
It’s been a bad couple of days to be a terrorist. GEORGE has in-depth coverage of the assassination of ISIS’ second-in-command and the Hamas leader who was an architect of the 7 October attacks on Israel.
Our @This Weekend in Brief news editor also has the details you should know about the Ebola outbreak as well as a look at intelligence gathered by Ukraine that shows Russia planning to mount new operations from Belarus and possibly even attack a NATO-member country.
For music fans, our @Fridell on Pop Culture columnist looks at the song that won this year’s Eurovision and delves into a brief history of how the Eurovision Song Contest came to be.
Meanwhile, don’t miss any of these stories in our Wednesday Morning Edition.
—Israel said that it had killed an architect of the 7 October attacks
—Swatch and Audemars Piguet introduced a pop-art-inspired timepiece that causes near stampedes at some Swatch retail shops
—Honda’s electric-vehicle woes become apparent in fiscal year 2025 earnings report
In addition, GEORGE has other exclusive news [including coverage of X and Y] in today’s edition so don’t touch that dial. Simply scroll down and read more GEORGE, starting with today’s editorial cartoon in The Sketch. GEORGE will be back tomorrow with a brand-new editorial cartoon, even more news, and stories you won’t find elsewhere.
Until then, remain curious!

@THE SKETCH
________________________________________________
IN THIS ISSUE
VOLUME VI… № 1,715
WELCOME (above)
@THE SKETCH (above) Eurovision Throughout the Years
IN THIS ISSUE
@INTERMEZZO I A couple in Kurashiki, Japan

@ABOUT GEORGE
____________________________________
@INTERMEZZO I
______________________________________
@THE WAR ROOM
— An Israeli air strike in Gaza on Friday killed Izz al-Din al-Haddad, the commander of Hamas’s armed wing. The late Mr. Al-Haddad was said to have been an architect of the 7 October attacks.
—Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that the United States’ “contradictory messages” destroyed his country’s “trust” in negotiations. He said the United States needed to get “serious.”
—On Friday Mr. Trump said a 20-year moratorium on Iran’s nuclear program would be enough for him to end the war, as opposed to his previous position, which was for Iran to surrender its nuclear ambitions.
—The USS Gerald Ford, the world’s largest aircraft-carrier, returned to port in Virginia after nearly a year at sea. The $13 billion ship was heavily involved in both the mission to capture Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela and the sorties against targets in Iran. Its deployment was the longest by an American carrier since the end of the Vietnam war. The previous record was held by the USS Midway, which was deployed for 332 days during the Vietnam War from 1972 to 1973.
—Israel and Lebanon agreed to extend their ceasefire for 45 days, the U.S. Department of State said. It described talks between the two sides in Washington on Thursday and Friday as “highly productive” even though there are almost daily reports of Hizbullah and Israel trading fire across southern Lebanon.
______________________________________
@INTERMEZZO II
______________________________________
@FRIEDELL ON POP CULTURE
Bulgaria Wins 70th Eurovision with Dance Anthem Bangaranga
Bravo, Bulgaria! The juries, televoters, and the Continent at large came together to support a song that sounds like three bangers fighting in a nightclub, thus resulting in Bulgaria’s first-ever Eurovision victory for singer Dara and the high-energy song Bangaranga. “Welcome to the riot” was not a mere lyric but far more, with the promise that “No one’s gonna sleep tonight.”
The track captivated audiences with its infectious beats, intense choreography, and a dynamic, sleekly framed stage production.
Meanwhile, Israel placed second with 343 points, for the song “Michelle,” performed by the Francophone singer Noam Bettan.
The Eurovision Song Contest is never predictable and that is just part of its charm. Also known as Concours Eurovision de la chanson or just «Eurovision», the contest was inspired by and based on the Italian Sanremo Music Festival, held in the Italian Riviera since 1951. Eurovision has been held annually since 1956. Germany has competed more times than any other country, having participated in all but one edition, while Ireland and Sweden hold the record for the most victories, with seven each.
Eurovision was organized by the European Broadcasting Union, based on an idea initially proposed by Radiotelevisione italiana manager Sergio Pugliese. Broadcasters from seven countries – Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Luxembourg, Netherlands, and Switzerland – participated in the first contest, with Austria, Denmark, and the United Kingdom joining the following year. In 1956, each country was represented by two songs; the only time in which multiple entries per country were permitted. The winning song was “Refrain”, representing the host country Switzerland and performed by Lys Assia.
Switzerland has won a total of three times including in the first year of the contest. In 1988, Céline Dion won with the song “Ne partez pas sans moi,” while in 2024, Nemo won with the song “The Code.”
Israel is a four-time Eurovision winner: “A-Ba-Ni-Bi” by Izhar Cohen and the Alphabeta won in 1978, “Hallelujah” by Milk and Honey won in 1979, “Diva” by Dana International won in 1998, and “Toy” by Netta Barzilai won most recently in 2018.
____________________________________
@INTERMEZZO III
____________________________________
@THIS WEEKEND IN BRIEF
Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia was planning to attack northern Ukraine or a North American Treaty Organization-member country that borders Belarus from Belarusian territory, such as Poland, Lithuania, or Latvia. Ukrainian intelligence has tracked efforts by Russia to draw Belarus deeper into the war and Mr. Zelensky said he received intelligence reports showing that the Kremlin had asked Alexander Lukashenko, Belarus’s president, to join “new Russian aggressive operations.” In addition, he said that Russia is believed to be utilizing newly constructed infrastructure, logistics routes, and artillery positions within Belarus to stage these potential operations.
____________________________________
The United States is reportedly preparing to indict Raúl Castro, Cuba’s former leader, over the 1996 downing of two civilian planes operated by the Miami-based Cuban exile group Brothers to the Rescue. The deadly attack, which occurred in international airspace, killed four people, including three American citizens. The move would further strain relations between the two countries as the island-nation recently announced it had run out of oil amidst a U.S.-led oil blockade, one of several measures intended to bring about regime change. Mr. Castro’s brother, Fidel Castro, first ceded his provisional powers to his brother in 2006 and announced his resignation from the presidency in 2008, at which point Raúl Castro was elected President of the Council of State and Council of Ministers, a position he held through 2018. He became First Secretary of the Communist Party of Cuba from 2011 after his brother stepped down from his official political post, to 2021.
____________________________________
Abu-Bilal al-Minuki, a senior leader of Islamic State, also known as ISIS, was killed in a joint Nigerian-U.S. operation in north-east Nigeria. In a statement, Mr. Trump said that “brave American forces and the Armed Forces of Nigeria flawlessly executed a meticulously planned and very complex mission to eliminate the most active terrorist in the world from the battlefield.” Mr. Minuki directed IS operations across the Sahel and west Africa. He was previously a prominent figure in another jihadist group, Boko Haram, and was directly linked to the mass kidnapping of 100 Nigerian schoolgirls in 2018.
____________________________________
The Islamic State, also known as the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant, the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria , and by its Arabic acronym Daesh, is a transnational Salafi jihadist militant organisation and internationally unrecognized quasi-state. It is designated as a terrorist organization by the United Nations and many countries around the world, including Muslim nations. At one point in the prior decade, the self-declared caliphate ruled an area with a population of about 12 million, where they enforced their extremist interpretation of Islamic law, managed an annual budget exceeding US$1 billion, and commanded more than 30,000 fighters. During its rule in Syria and Iraq, the group became notorious for its brutality. It committed genocides against Yazidis and Iraqi Turkmen; engaged in persecution of Christians, Shia Muslims, and Mandaeans; publicized videos of beheadings of soldiers, journalists, and aid workers; and decimated cultural sites. The group has perpetrated terrorist massacres in territories outside of its control, such as the November 2015 Paris attacks, in which three suicide bombers struck outside the Stade de France in Saint-Denis during an international football match, another group of attackers then fired on crowded cafés and restaurants in Paris, and a third group carried out another mass shooting and took hostages at an Eagles of Death Metal concert attended by 1,500 people in the Bataclan theatre, leading to a stand-off with police. The attackers killed 130 people, including 90 who were in the Bataclan, and 416 were injured, ca. 100 critically. Another similar attack was the 2024 Crocus City Hall music venue attack in Russia, in which 151 people were killed and 609 were injured, one of the deadliest attacks ever to take place on Russian soil.
____________________________________
____________________________________
The Long Island Rail Road, the busiest passenger rail service in North America, shut down on Saturday after unions and transit officials failed to agree on a new contract. Some 3,500 members of five unions that represent engineers, signalmen, and machinists, walked off the job at midnight (00:00) local time on 16 May, as three years of failed contract negotiations came to a head. New York State Governor Kathy Hochul called into the negotiations on Friday to express her view that “nobody wins in a strike.” She told the negotiators that riders would suffer and thousands of workers would lose out on pay, Sean Butler, a spokesman for the governor, said. The strike on the Long Island Rail Road, which carries more than 270,000 passengers a day between Long Island and New York City, on average, is expected to cause chaos for travelers with few other options. Many commuters rely on the service as do visitors to New York City and all of its cultural and culinary offerings, while many visitors to the region use the railroad to explore Long Island, a densely populated continental island that extends into the Atlantic Ocean which still maintains the charm of what was once almost entirely backwoods and farms. Long Island offers some of the finest beaches, golf courses, open-air concert venues, and restaurants in the region.
____________________________________
Police were on high alert in London as they expected a very busy day with two major demonstrations and the FA Cup final taking place. Tens of thousands of people gathered in London for the two rival marches: one led by Tommy Robinson, a far-right activist, the other marking the anniversary of the displacement of Palestinians when Israel was created in 1948. Around 4,000 police officers were on the streets of London, where the two marches took place. Thousands of police officers and facial recognition were used in what officials termed an “unprecedented” operation. Despite the crowds, police arrested a total of 31 protesters across both marches, which passed “largely without significant incident.” Approximately 20,000 people attended the pro-Palestine protest, while around 60,000 attended the Unite The Kingdom protest, it is understood.
____________________________________
Manchester City beat Chelsea 1-0 in the FA Cup, the last match in the Football Association Challenge Cup. at Wembley on Saturday. The team’s manager, Pep Guardiola, said on Saturday his players would not be allowed “even one beer” to celebrate their FA Cup success as his attention turned immediately to the crucial Premier League clash with Bournemouth, which will be on Tuesday.
____________________________________
Celtic have clinched their 14th Scottish Premiership title in 15 years, and denied Hearts their first since 1960, after a dramatic 3-1 win saw them beat their title rivals in Glasgow on Saturday. The win booked Celtic a Champions League playoff spot for next season.
____________________________________
On the heels of Mr. Trump’s state visit to Beijing, Taiwan pushed for continued access to U.S. military supplies. Sales of American arms “serve as a mutual deterrence against regional threats”, said a Taiwanese government spokeswoman. Mr Trump had earlier said he would soon “make a determination” as to whether to continue such sales, but “made no commitment either way.”
____________________________________
____________________________________
An Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has resulted in the death of 65 people. Nearly 250 cases have been reported in the Ituri province on the border with Uganda and South Sudan. The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Africa’s health agency, warned that it could spread rapidly because of intense population movement in the area. It is the 17th outbreak of the deadly virus in the country since 1976. Ebola presents as a zoonotic viral hemorrhagic fever in humans and other primates, caused by four of the six known Ebola viruses. The 2013–2016 epidemic of Ebola virus disease, centered in West Africa, was the most widespread outbreak of the disease in history, with 28,616 people who became infected and a death toll of 11,310, for a case-mortality rate of 40%.
____________________________________
Swatch stores across the globe were forced to shutter their doors as crowds of customers sought to buy the new Royal Pop watches made by Swatch and Audemars Piguet, two Swiss watchmakers. Long queues had formed in recent days of people eager for the much-hyped pop-art-inspired timepieces, priced at around $400, but the swarm of customers forced shops in Britain, France, India, and the United Arab Emirates among others to lock their doors. The Royal Pop is a highly anticipated, modular 2-in-1 pocket and wristwatch collaboration between Audemars Piguet and Swatch that blends Audemars Piguet’s iconic 1972 Royal Oak design with the playful, pop-art style of Swatch. The timepiece features a click-in, pop-out case design suspended on a calfskin lanyard.
____________________________________
Bond yields surged around the world, fueled by concerns over inflation. Yields on America’s ten-year Treasuries rose above 4.5%, to their highest level in more than a year. Borrowing costs on Japan’s 30-year debt exceeded 4% for the first time. The sell-off extended to stock markets. America’s NASDAQ index posted its first weekly loss in more than a month.
____________________________________
@INTERMEZZO IV
____________________________________
@BARTLEBY ON LANGUAGE
“Beware the Thucydides Trap, My Son!”
If Charles Lutwidge Dodgson, who wrote under the pen name Lewis Carroll, had been a scholar of Ancient Greece, instead of a 19th century author of children’s books such as Alice in Wonderland, he might have given thought to the observation by Thucydides in his History of the Peloponnesian War that “it was the rise of Athens and the fear that this instilled in Sparta that made war inevitable.”
Instead, he concentrated on books such as Through the Looking Glass, which included his poem “Jabberwocky.”
“Beware the Jabberwock, my son,” he wrote, warning the hero to avoid a terrifying, mythical beast. The poem symbolizes a warning against confronting hidden, dangerous evil or, more broadly, a prompt to prepare for daunting challenges, often using nonsense language to enhance its whimsical yet ominous tone
Some 128 years after Mr. Carroll’s death, political scientist Graham Allison used the term “Thucydides Trap” to describe a tendency towards war when a rising power – Athens is a good example – challenges the status of a ruling power, e.g. Sparta. Mr. Allison expanded his thoughts on the trap rather significantly in his 2017 book Destined for War, in which he argued that “China and the United States are currently on a collision course for war.”
In greeting Mr. Trump in China, Chinese leader Xi Jinping invoked this warning from the Classical world, when saying that the United States and China should beware the “Thucydides Trap” in their own relations.
Pundits including GEORGE’s own Jonathan Spira have said that Mr. Trump might have done better with the Jabberwocky reference, we’ll have to wait on this as only time will tell.
____________________________________
@INTERMEZZO V
______________________________________
@WEDGWOOD ON FINANCE
Honda Motor reported its first annual operating loss since becoming a publicly-traded company in 1957. The automaker said it lost ¥414.3 billion ($2.6 billion) in fiscal year 2025 ended March 2025. The Japanese carmaker has struggled with increased competition from China and a failed bet on electric vehicles, for which demand has fallen. This resulted in massive restructuring charges, battery plant writedowns, and halted investments including the construction of its massive $11 billion EV and battery project in Canada. The company, which is also the world’s largest motorcycle manufacturer, plans to pivot back to a focus on mixed powertrains, hybrid vehicles, and internal-combustion engines. Despite the auto division’s losses, its motorcycle division achieved record-high sales, driven by strong markets in India and Brazil, which helped cushion the the financial blow.
____________________________________
@RECENT DISPATCHES OF NOTE
A so-called “super” El Niño is increasingly likely to form in late 2026 and it will likely be one of the strongest on record. The potential for dangerous conditions to form has prompted multiple comparisons to the El Niño from 1877, when such an event resulted in catastrophic conditions across the globe. El Niño, or “Little Boy” in English, is a naturally occurring climate pattern characterized by the warming of ocean surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean. It typically occurs every two to seven years and significantly disrupts global weather and marine conditions. This phenomenon is expected to bring hotter, drier weather to parts of Asia and Australia and may influence Atlantic hurricane activity in the Americas. The southern United States may see a wetter winter, while the event will increase the risk of drought in other regions.
______________________________________
The Cuban government said on Thursday that the island-nation’s oil reserves have run dry. The news follows months of ongoing energy crises that have led to significant power outages. Now, it is likely to plunge the country into a new phase in which a lack of electrical power is the rule, not the exception. “We have absolutely no fuel oil, absolutely no diesel,” Vicente de la O Levy, Cuba’s minister of energy and mines, said in a statement. “In Havana, the blackouts today exceed 20 or 22 hours.” Cuba has faced a severe energy crisis for over two years, a result of aging infrastructure in need of replacement and an ever-decreasing supply from Venezuela, which has been the country’s primary source of fossil fuel.

By Faith Anisiobi, The Sight News

sources.news_title: U.S. Kills ISIS Second-in-Command in Nigeria Strike
sources.text:
President Donald Trump announced late Friday that American and Nigerian forces killed Abu-Bilal al-Minuki, the man U.S. officials described as ISIS's second-in-command worldwide, in a joint military operation in northeastern Nigeria. No U.S. service members were harmed.
Trump disclosed the strike on Truth Social, calling it "a meticulously planned and very complex mission to eliminate the most active terrorist in the world from the battlefield." U.S. Africa Command confirmed the operation in a formal statement Saturday, reporting that its initial assessment found multiple terrorists, including al-Minuki and other senior ISIS leaders, were killed on May 16, 2026.
The strike caps months of intelligence gathering and military coordination between Washington and the Nigerian government, and it marks the highest-profile counterterrorism operation on African soil during Trump's second term. It also sends a pointed message: the administration is willing to project lethal force well beyond the Middle Eastern theater where most recent anti-ISIS campaigns have played out.
Secretary of War Pete Hegseth identified al-Minuki in a Saturday morning post on X as "the senior ISIS General Directorate of Provinces Emir, the number two for ISIS globally, responsible for overseeing the planning of attacks, directing hostage-taking and managing financial operations." AFRICOM's own statement called him "the director of global operations for ISIS" and "the most active terrorist in the world."
The command added that al-Minuki provided "strategic guidance to the ISIS global network on media and financial operations as well as the development and manufacturing of weapons, explosives, and drones." He was not a figurehead. By every official account, he ran the day-to-day machinery of a terror network still capable of killing Americans and targeting Christians across West Africa.
Just The News reported that a 2023 State Department bulletin had already identified al-Minuki as an ISIS leader, and the Treasury Department had sanctioned him as a specially designated global terrorist. He had been on the radar for years. The question was always when, and where, he could be reached.
The answer turned out to be Africa. Trump put it bluntly on Truth Social:
"Abu-Bilal al-Minuki, second in command of ISIS globally, thought he could hide in Africa, but little did he know we had sources who kept us informed on what he was doing."
AFRICOM's Saturday statement laid out the chain of authority. Fox News Digital reported the command's language: "At the direction of the President of the United States and the Secretary of War, and in coordination with the Government of Nigeria, U.S. Africa Command conducted an operation against ISIS in Northeastern Nigeria on May 16, 2026."
AFRICOM commander U.S. Air Force Gen. Dagvin Anderson praised the partnership with Nigeria's armed forces, stating that the mission "was made possible through the cooperation and coordination of our forces in recent months."
Anderson added a warning:
"Make no mistake, our two nations will relentlessly pursue and neutralize terrorist threats and are committed to protecting our people and interests."
Hegseth said AFRICOM carried out the "precise operation to remove this terrorist" at Trump's direction and in conjunction with Nigeria's president. He framed the strike not just as a tactical win but as a fulfillment of a specific presidential pledge, one that linked counterterrorism to the protection of persecuted Christians in Nigeria.
The administration had previously signaled that protecting Christians under threat from Islamist violence in West Africa was a policy priority. Hegseth made the connection explicit, saying Trump had "declared to the world that we will help protect Christians in Nigeria and instructed the Department of War to prepare for action." That preparation, by Hegseth's account, lasted months.
"So, for months, we hunted this top ISIS leader in Nigeria who was killing Christians, and we killed him, and his entire posse."
That line from the Secretary of War captures the administration's tone, direct, unapologetic, and deliberate. This was not a reactive strike. It was a hunt.
The Nigeria operation did not happen in a vacuum. It fits into a sustained and escalating campaign against ISIS that has stretched across multiple theaters since late 2025.
On December 13, 2025, an ISIS ambush in Palmyra, Syria, killed two U.S. service members and an American interpreter. That attack triggered Operation Hawkeye Strike, under which the U.S. military carried out ten strikes against more than 30 ISIS targets in Syria. By February, U.S. Central Command announced that more than 50 ISIS terrorists had been killed or captured and more than 100 ISIS infrastructure targets struck during two months of targeted operations in Syria.
The administration's willingness to absorb losses and respond with overwhelming force has defined its counterterrorism posture. The Palmyra ambush was a painful reminder that ISIS remains lethal. The response, sustained, methodical, and geographically expanding, reflects a counterterrorism leadership structure that prizes follow-through over press conferences.
Trump himself referenced the broader regional picture when he told reporters on January 27 that he had a "great conversation" with Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa. "All of the things having to do with Syria in that area are working out very, very well," Trump said. "So, we are very happy about it."
The strike in northeastern Nigeria signals that the administration views the ISIS threat as genuinely global, not confined to Syria and Iraq, where the group first seized territory a decade ago. Nigeria has faced years of violence from Boko Haram and the Islamic State of West Africa Province, an ISIS affiliate that has terrorized communities across the Lake Chad Basin.
The Washington Examiner reported that the operation took place in the Lake Chad Basin and was overseen by AFRICOM with no American casualties. Defense officials told reporters that al-Minuki had been hunted for months and that his removal would weaken ISIS's global operations.
The New York Post noted that the U.S. had recently increased pressure and military involvement in Nigeria, including prior airstrikes and the deployment of about 200 American troops. That footprint is small by historical standards, but the results speak for themselves: a months-long intelligence operation that located and eliminated the most senior ISIS figure outside the group's traditional strongholds.
The partnership with Nigeria deserves attention. Joint operations of this kind require trust, shared intelligence, and compatible rules of engagement. Anderson's statement credited "the cooperation and coordination of our forces in recent months" as the foundation for the strike. That kind of language from a combatant commander is not boilerplate, it reflects real operational integration.
Trump declared on Truth Social that "with his removal, ISIS's global operation is greatly diminished." Hegseth echoed the assessment, stating that "the removal of him and other ISIS personnel makes Americans safer by further degrading ISIS's ability to plan and carry out attacks that threaten the U.S. homeland, American citizens, and innocent civilians."
Terrorist organizations have survived the loss of senior leaders before. But al-Minuki was not merely a symbolic figure. He ran attack planning, hostage operations, and financial networks. He oversaw weapons manufacturing and drone development. Replacing that operational expertise is not like appointing a new spokesman.
The fact that multiple other senior ISIS leaders were also killed in the same strike compounds the damage. AFRICOM's initial assessment described "multiple terrorists" eliminated alongside al-Minuki. The exact number has not been disclosed, but the command's language suggests this was not a single-target operation. It was a systematic dismantling of a leadership node.
The administration's approach to crisis planning and presidential authority has drawn scrutiny from various quarters, but the Nigeria strike illustrates a model that is hard to argue with on results: clear presidential direction, patient intelligence work, a capable partner nation, and decisive force.
Several details remain unclear. The exact location within northeastern Nigeria has not been publicly identified beyond the Lake Chad Basin region. The specific U.S. and Nigerian units involved have not been named. And the total number of ISIS leaders killed alongside al-Minuki has not been disclosed.
Fox News Digital reported that it reached out to the White House for comment. AFRICOM released video footage showing targeted strikes against ISIS fighters, though the full contents of that footage have not been described in detail.
The administration's broader use of presidential power continues to generate debate across Washington. But on the narrow question of whether the United States can still find and eliminate the world's most dangerous terrorists, even when they flee to Africa, the answer from northeastern Nigeria is unambiguous.
Hegseth closed his Saturday statement with a line that doubles as both a promise and a warning:
"This should serve as a reminder that we will hunt down those who wish to harm Americans or innocent Christians, wherever they are."
The internal dynamics of the administration's national security team have drawn plenty of attention in recent months. But whatever the personnel debates, the operational results in Nigeria speak plainly: the people tasked with finding and finishing ISIS leaders are doing their jobs.
Terrorists who think distance equals safety just lost their best argument.

sources.news_title: Top IS commander Abu Bilal Al-Minuki killed, says Trump
sources.text:
New Delhi, May 16: In a daredevil operation, global leader of the Islamic State (IS), Abu Bilal Al-Minuki, was killed in a joint operation conducted by the United States and Nigerian security forces last night.
“American forces and the Armed Forces of Nigeria flawlessly executed a meticulously planned and highly complex mission to eliminate the most active terrorist in the world from the battlefield,” President Trump said.
“He will no longer terrorize the people of Africa or help plan operations targeting Americans,” Trump added. “With his removal, ISIS’s global operation is greatly diminished.”
Trump thanked the government of Nigeria for its “partnership” in the operation, while not disclosing the exact location where it took place.
The U.S. State Department described Al-Minuki as a Sahel-based IS senior leader and part of the group’s General Directorate of Provinces, the administrative body that provides operational guidance and funding worldwide.
IS has radically shifted in recent years, with around 90% of its attacks now taking place in sub-Saharan Africa. Its Nigeria-based branch is by far the most active.
Nigerian President Bola Tinubu said the two countries had carried out a “daring joint operation that dealt a heavy blow” to IS.
Al-Minuki was declared a Specially Designated Global Terrorist by Washington in 2023. He had reportedly been promoted to “Head of the General Directorate of States,” making him one of the most senior figures within the global IS hierarchy.

sources.news_title: US-Nigeria Joint Operation Kills Senior ISIS Commander Abubakar Mainok
sources.text:
United States President Donald Trump has announced the successful killing of Abubakar Mainok, a senior commander within the Islamic State described as the organization’s global second-in-command. The operation, which the president characterized as a “meticulously planned and very complex mission,” was carried out through a direct partnership between the U.S. And the Nigerian government.
The removal of Mainok, also known as Abu-Bilal al-Mainuki, marks a critical escalation in the effort to dismantle the Islamic State’s infrastructure across Africa. In a statement shared by the White House on X, President Trump praised the bilateral cooperation, asserting that the operation had effectively removed “the most active terrorist in the world from the battlefield.”
The operation represents a tangible result of a renewed and intensified counterterrorism collaboration between Washington and Abuja. This security pivot follows a period of significant diplomatic friction, during which President Trump raised concerns over what he described as “Christian genocide” in the region, eventually leading to the deployment of approximately 200 U.S. Troops to Nigeria to bolster local capacities.
The Profile of Abu-Bilal al-Mainuki
Abubakar Mainok was a high-value target for international intelligence agencies long before this mission. According to U.S. Government registers, Mainok was officially designated as a “global terrorist” in 2023. Intelligence documents trace his origins to the town of Mainok, located within the Kaga Local Government Area of Borno State, a region that has remained a primary flashpoint for insurgency in North-east Nigeria.
Security analysts and intelligence reports have consistently linked Mainok to the strategic coordination of Islamic State operations throughout West Africa and the Sahel. A 2023 report by the Jamestown Foundation identified him as a pivotal figure responsible for bridging the gap between the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) and the broader IS-Sahel networks. He reportedly operated through the group’s al-Furqan office, the wing responsible for the organization’s official communications and strategic propaganda.
By serving as a conduit between these two powerful regional franchises, Mainok was instrumental in synchronizing tactical movements and resource sharing, making him one of the most dangerous operational figures in the region.
A Strategic Shift in U.S.-Nigeria Relations
The joint operation comes at a time of evolving diplomatic dynamics between the United States and Nigeria. The deployment of U.S. Personnel to the West African nation was not without controversy, following a public diplomatic faceoff regarding human rights and the protection of religious minorities. However, the shared goal of neutralizing the Islamic State’s leadership appears to have bridged these divides.
While the Nigerian government has yet to issue a formal public statement regarding the specifics of the mission, sources familiar with the operation have confirmed that the strike took place in the North-east, the heartland of ISWAP’s influence. The precision of the strike suggests a high level of intelligence sharing, blending U.S. Surveillance capabilities with Nigerian ground intelligence.
The impact of this operation can be understood through the lens of the current security architecture in the region:
| Element | Pre-Operation Status | Post-Operation Impact |
|---|---|---|
| IS Command Structure | Centralized coordination via al-Furqan office | Significant leadership vacuum at the global level |
| U.S.-Nigeria Ties | Diplomatic tension over human rights | Proven tactical interoperability |
| Regional Stability | Active ISWAP/IS-Sahel synchronization | Disruption of cross-border terror logistics |
The Broader Fight Against ISWAP and IS-Sahel
The death of Mainok is a blow to the Islamic State’s “Wilayat” (provinces) in Africa, but it occurs against a backdrop of persistent instability. The Islamic State West Africa Province continues to challenge the Nigerian state, often competing for dominance with the Boko Haram faction. The ability of ISWAP to maintain a sophisticated administrative structure—including the al-Furqan office—has allowed it to govern territory and recruit more effectively than many of its contemporaries.
By targeting the “global second-in-command,” the U.S. And Nigeria are signaling a shift from containment to the active decapitation of the group’s leadership. This strategy aims to create internal chaos within the organization, forcing remaining commanders to prioritize their own survival over the planning of attacks.
The operation underscores the importance of the U.S. Department of State‘s focus on regional security partners to prevent the Sahel from becoming a permanent sanctuary for global jihadist movements. With the removal of a key coordinator, the hope is that the link between the West African and Sahelian cells will be permanently severed.
The next critical milestone will be the official confirmation and detailed briefing from the Nigerian military command, which is expected to outline the broader implications for the security of Borno State and the surrounding border regions.
We invite our readers to share their perspectives on the evolving security landscape in West Africa in the comments below.

sources.news_title: ISIS Terror Kingpin Executed In Midnight Raid – Trump Delivers On Promise To Protect Nigeria's Christians
sources.text:
U.S. and Nigerian forces killed ISIS global second-in-command Abu-Bilal al-Minuki in a nighttime raid in Nigeria, officials said Saturday.
The joint operation took place late Friday, May 15, striking a remote compound where al-Minuki and several other senior ISIS figures were meeting inside an established fortified base in the area, in Metele, Borno state.
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth confirmed the death in a brief statement, calling it a direct result of President Donald Trump’s orders last November to target ISIS leaders threatening Christians in the region.
“President Trump pledged to protect these communities, and our forces delivered,” Hegseth said. “Al-Minuki is no longer in a position to plan attacks or fund terror.”
Al-Minuki oversaw key parts of ISIS operations worldwide. Intelligence officials say he directed attack planning, managed hostage situations, and moved money across ISIS networks.
Huge Blow to ISIS
His death marks one of the biggest blows to the group since its territorial losses in Iraq and Syria years ago.
The raid unfolded under the cover of darkness as American special operations forces worked alongside Nigerian troops, using precise intelligence to hit the target without warning.
Officials said the operation was clean and there were no U.S. or Nigerian casualties.
Trump’s first strong condemnation of Nigeria came in November 2025, after a series of attacks on Christian villages that left dozens dead.
ISIS-linked fighters in the northeast and other militant groups had stepped up killings, church burnings, and kidnappings.
Trump called the violence against Christians unacceptable and ordered the Pentagon to prepare targeted action.
Also Read: Hormuz Crisis Escalates as US Rejects Iran Warship Claim
Nigeria has struggled for years with multiple insurgencies. Boko Haram and its ISIS-aligned splinter groups have killed thousands and displaced many more.
Christians in the north and Middle Belt have been hit especially hard, with entire communities forced to flee. Local leaders have long asked for stronger international help.
Friday’s success comes as Trump pushes a tougher approach to terrorism. Unlike past administrations that often focused on U.S. large-scale missions or drone strikes from afar, this operation mixed U.S. special forces with local troops.
Hegseth said the elimination of Abu-Bilal al-Minuki is a big win in the U.S. fight aginst against terrorism and leaves the terror group with a massive gap to fill.
“He wasn’t just a figurehead. This guy moved money, approved plans, and kept the network alive,” he said. “Taking him out disrupts their finances and their command chain at the same time.”
Also Read: Trump DOJ Moves to Revoke Citizenship of 12 Over Alleged Terrorism, Abuse, and Fraud
U.S. officials told the BBC that intelligence had established that Minuki had established a fortified base in the area, in Metele, Borno state.
They confirmed he was actively plotting threats against Nigerian civilians and Western interests more broadly.
Several mid-level commanders died alongside al-Minuki, further weakening the group’s remaining structure in West Africa.
Christians in Nigeria welcomed the news, with some believers saying the raid offers real hope after years of fear.
However, not everyone is celebrating in Nigeria; some are worried that more U.S. involvement could spark revenge attacks or stir up anti-Western feelings.
Others question whether one raid can change the bigger picture of instability, poverty, and weak governance that lets militants survive.
Trump Hails Successful Operation
Trump, taking to social media shortly after the operation’s success, thanked the government of Nigeria for their effective cooperation in the mission.
“Abu-Bilal al-Minuki thought he could hide in Africa, but little did he know we had sources who kept us informed on what he was doing.
“He will no longer terrorize the people of Africa or help plan operations to target Americans,” Trump said.
The Pentagon plans to keep pressure on remaining ISIS networks in the region, with more operations expected based on fresh intelligence.
